entry: American labor leader and feminist activist. With [[Cesar Chavez]] and Gilbert Padilla she co-founded the National Farm Workers Association, which became the United Farm Workers (UFW). She managed boycott campaigns during the 1965 Delano grape strike. Some credit her with the slogan *sí se puede* ("yes we can"). She later campaigned for women's reproductive rights and worked with the Feminist Majority Foundation to help Latina women become more active in politics. In 2002 she founded the Dolores Huerta Foundation in [[Bakersfield, California]]. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012.

Any of 40 extant species of toothed aquatic mammal in several [[Cetacean|cetacean]] families, closely related to [[Whale|whales]] and [[Porpoise|porpoises]]. Dolphins range from Maui's dolphin, about 1.7 m long and 50 kg, to the [[Orca|orca]], up to 9.5 m long and 10 tonnes, an [[Apex predator|apex predator]]. Their forelimbs evolved into flippers, their hindlimbs are lost, and their tail forms a horizontal fluke. Most species live in warm tropical waters, though some inhabit brackish or fresh water. They are carnivorous, feeding largely on fish and [[Squid|squid]], and a few large species prey on seals and other dolphins and porpoises. Dolphins live in fluid social groups called pods and communicate with high-pitched clicks and whistles, using echolocation. They are hunted in [[Japan]] and parts of [[Latin America]], and face threats from bycatch and pollution.

Highest rank in [[Taxonomy (biology)|biological taxonomy]], grouping all organisms. It was introduced in the three-domain system devised by Carl Woese, Otto Kandler and Mark Wheelis in 1990, which divides life into [[Archaea]], [[Bacteria]] and Eukarya. Archaea and Bacteria are [[Prokaryote|prokaryotes]], single-celled microorganisms without a membrane-bound nucleus, while organisms with a [[Cell nucleus|cell nucleus]] and other membrane-bound organelles belong to Eukarya and are called [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]]. Woese identified the three branches in 1977 by comparing [[RNA|ribosomal RNA]] sequences, and the two prokaryotic domains differ in membrane chemistry and RNA markers. Alternatives include a two-domain system that places Eukarya within Archaea, and the earlier two-empire system of Prokaryota and Eukaryota. Non-cellular life, including [[Virus|viruses]], is excluded.

Architectural element similar to the hollow upper half of a [[Sphere|sphere]]. A dome may rest on a rotunda wall, a drum, or squinches or pendentives that carry the transition from a square or polygonal base to a round one. Its apex may be open as an oculus. Domes were built in [[Mesopotamia]] and appear in Persian, Hellenistic, Roman and Chinese architecture. Dome structures were common in [[Byzantine architecture|Byzantine]] and Sasanian architecture, influencing Europe and Islam in the [[Middle Ages]]. The domes of [[Renaissance architecture|European Renaissance architecture]] spread from Italy in the early modern period. [[Filippo Brunelleschi]]'s octagonal dome of [[Florence Cathedral]], built from 1420 to 1436 without temporary wooden centering, spanned 45.5 m. In the 20th century, [[Buckminster Fuller|R. Buckminster Fuller]] popularized the geodesic dome. Domes have been built from mud, stone, wood, brick, concrete, metal and glass.

Manuscript record of the Great Survey of much of [[England]] and parts of Wales, historically believed to have been completed in 1086 at the behest of [[William the Conqueror]]. Research by the medievalist Carol Symes indicates that it may have been completed as late as 1098–1114. The survey recorded the annual value of each landed property and the resources from which that value derived. The name alludes to the Last Judgment and the unalterable character of the book's decisions. The manuscript is held at the National Archives in Kew, London, and is an invaluable source for economic historians.

Large domesticated fowl, *Meleagris gallopavo domesticus*, of the same species as the [[Wild turkey|wild turkey]]. Domestication is thought to have occurred in central [[Mesoamerica]] at least 2,000 years ago, where people used its meat, eggs and feathers. The [[Aztecs]] associated the bird with the trickster god Tezcatlipoca. Its main modern varieties descend from turkeys that the Spanish took from central Mexico to Europe in the 16th century. English navigator William Strickland is credited with introducing it to [[England]]. [[Intensive farming]] from the late 1940s sharply cut its price, and most birds are bred with white feathers, whose pin feathers are less visible on the dressed carcass. Turkeys were sent from England to [[Jamestown]], Virginia, in 1608. In Canada and the United States males are called toms; in the United Kingdom and Ireland, stags.

Violence or abuse within a domestic setting, such as a marriage or [[Cohabitation|cohabitation]]. The term is often used as a synonym for [[Intimate relationship|intimate partner violence]]. Abuse takes physical, verbal, emotional, financial, reproductive and sexual forms, and in 2015 the United Kingdom's Home Office widened the definition to include coercive control. The World Health Organization estimates that one in three women experience such violence at some point in their lives. It is among the most underreported crimes for both men and women, and victims may develop [[Post-traumatic stress disorder|post-traumatic stress disorder]]. Worldwide, women are the overwhelming majority of victims and experience more severe forms. Studies using the Conflict Tactics Scale, however, find comparable rates of physical aggression by men and women in many relationships. Critics argue that policy focus on female victims overlooks male victims and female-perpetrated aggression.

Person who works within a residence and performs household services for an employer, such as cleaning, cooking, laundry, ironing or caring for children and elderly dependents. Some domestic workers live in the household. The work is often undervalued and poorly regulated, and in many jurisdictions domestic workers suffer serious abuses, including [[Slavery|slavery]]. The older English term is *servant*. In Britain, domestic service peaked towards the close of the [[Victorian era]], a period known in the [[United States]] as the [[Gilded Age]] and in France as the [[Belle Époque]]. Its Edwardian form was highly hierarchical, reflecting limited social mobility before [[World War I]].

Set of behaviors, customs and rituals, abbreviated D/s, involving the submission of one person to another in an erotic episode or lifestyle. It is a subset of [[BDSM]]. Physical contact is not necessary, and it can be conducted anonymously by telephone or email. Both parties take pleasure from dominating or being dominated. Those in the superior position are called dominants (Doms or Dommes), and those in the subordinate position are called submissives or subs. A switch plays either role. Some practices cross into [[Sadomasochism|sadomasochism]].

Woman who takes the dominant role in [[BDSM]] activities, usually as a paid professional. The practice is called female dominance, or femdom. Dominatrices are popularly known for inflicting physical pain, but not in every case; [[Erotic humiliation|erotic humiliation]], such as verbal humiliation or humiliating tasks, is also used. A dominatrix may be of any sexual orientation, which does not limit the genders of her submissive partners. The word derives from [[Latin]] *domina*, meaning "mistress" or "lady of the house."

Island country (pop., 2011: 71,293) in the Windward Islands of the [[Lesser Antilles]], in the [[Caribbean]]. Covering 750 sq km, it is the youngest island in the Lesser Antilles and is still being formed by volcanic activity. Known as the "Nature Island of the Caribbean," it has lush rainforests and [[Hot spring|hot springs]], including Boiling Lake, the world's second-largest hot spring. The island was settled by Arawak and later Kalinago peoples, and [[Christopher Columbus]] passed it in 1493. France colonized it from 1690 to 1763, bringing enslaved West Africans to work on coffee plantations, and Britain took control after the [[Seven Years' War]]. Dominica became an independent republic in 1978. The critically endangered Sisserou parrot, found only on the island, appears on the national flag, one of two sovereign national flags featuring purple. The country belongs to the [[Commonwealth of Nations]] and the [[United Nations]].

Island country (pop., 2024: 11.4 million) occupying the eastern part of [[Hispaniola]], in the [[Caribbean]]. It is the second-largest country in the Antilles by area, after [[Cuba]], at 48,671 sq km. [[Christopher Columbus]] claimed the island for Castile in 1492, and the colony of [[Santo Domingo]] became the first permanent European settlement in the Americas. Independence from Spain, declared in 1821, was followed by annexation by [[Haiti|Haiti]], and independence was finally won in 1844. The United States occupied the country from 1916 to 1924, and the dictatorship of [[Rafael Trujillo]] lasted from 1930 until his assassination in 1961. Since 1996 it has moved toward [[Democracy|representative democracy]]. Construction, manufacturing, tourism and mining drive an economy that is the largest in the Caribbean, and the country is the most visited destination in the region.

Family of tile-based games played with rectangular pieces, each divided into two square ends marked with pips (spots) or left blank. The traditional European set has 28 tiles showing every combination of spot counts from zero to six. The earliest mention is in *Former Events in Wulin* by Zhou Mi, from [[Song dynasty|Song dynasty]] China. Modern dominoes first appeared in [[France]] in the mid-18th century, but there is no confirmed link to the Chinese game. The name probably derives from a black-hooded costume worn during the Venetian Carnival. A set, like [[Dice|dice]] or playing cards, can be used for many games. Popular games include Domino Whist, Matador, Muggins (All Fives), Texas 42 and Mexican Train. In Britain, Fives and Threes is the most popular league and pub game. Dominoes have also been used for divination, such as bone throwing in Chinese culture.

[[Roman emperor]] (r. 81–96), the last member of the Flavian dynasty. He was the son of Vespasian and younger brother of Titus, and was declared emperor by the Praetorian Guard after Titus's death. His 15-year reign was the longest since [[Tiberius]]. He revalued the coinage, strengthened the frontiers and began a large building program to restore [[Rome]]. His general Agricola advanced in Caledonia (Scotland), but in Dacia Domitian was unable to defeat King [[Decebalus]] decisively. [[Propaganda]] fostered a [[Cult of personality|cult of personality]], and he named himself perpetual censor. He was popular with the people and army but considered a tyrant by the Senate. Senatorial writers, including [[Tacitus]], Pliny the Younger and Suetonius, portrayed him as a cruel and paranoid tyrant, while modern historians have offered more favorable assessments. He was [[Assassination|assassinated]] by court officials in 96 and succeeded the same day by Nerva.

Australian cricketer, widely acknowledged as the greatest batsman of all time. His career Test batting average of 99.94 is considered by some the greatest achievement by any sportsman in any major sport. He scored at a consistently high level over a 20-year playing career; former Australian captain Bill Woodfull said he was "worth three batsmen to Australia." England devised the controversial Bodyline tactics to curb his scoring. After the [[World War II|Second World War]] he captained an Australian team known as the "Invincibles" on a record-breaking unbeaten tour of England. After retiring he worked for three decades as an administrator, selector and writer. In 1997 Prime Minister John Howard called him the "greatest living Australian."

Two-act *dramma giocoso* by [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart]], with an Italian libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte. It is based on the Spanish legend of the libertine Don Juan, as told in Tirso de Molina's 1630 play *El burlador de Sevilla*. The opera premiered in Prague on October 29, 1787, and blends comedy, melodrama and supernatural elements. In the plot, Don Giovanni kills the father of one of his conquests and is dragged to hell by the animated statue of the slain Commendatore. It is regarded as one of the greatest works of the [[Opera|opera]] repertoire, ranks among the most frequently performed operas, and has inspired adaptations including by [[Franz Liszt]].

American actor and singer-songwriter. He played undercover detective James "Sonny" Crockett in the television series *[[Miami Vice]]*, for which he won a Golden Globe Award. He also starred in the title role of *Nash Bridges*. Johnson received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 1996. His films include *A Boy and His Dog* (1975) and *Knives Out* (2019). His cover of "Heartbeat" peaked at number five on the Billboard Hot 100.

American [[Boxing|boxing]] promoter known for a flamboyant style. King promoted "The Rumble in the Jungle," between [[Muhammad Ali]] and [[George Foreman]], and the "Thrilla in Manila," between Ali and [[Joe Frazier]]. His fighters included [[Mike Tyson]] and [[Evander Holyfield]], and several boxers sued him for allegedly defrauding them. King was convicted in 1967 of killing an employee, a conviction reduced on appeal to voluntary manslaughter. A 1954 fatal shooting had been ruled justifiable homicide.

American actor and comedian. He is best known for playing Deputy Barney Fife on the 1960s sitcom *The Andy Griffith Show*, for which he won five Emmy Awards. He later played the landlord Ralph Furley on *[[Three's Company]]* from 1979 to 1984. He starred in comedies including *The Incredible Mr. Limpet* (1964) and *The Ghost and Mr. Chicken* (1966). While serving in the Army during the [[World War II|Second World War]], he became a ventriloquist and comedian in a G.I. variety show.

Novel in two parts, published in 1605 and 1615, by [[Miguel de Cervantes]]. Written in Early Modern Spanish, it follows the hidalgo Alonso Quijano of La Mancha, who reads so many [[Chivalry|chivalric]] romances that he becomes a knight-errant under the name Don Quixote to revive chivalry. He recruits the farm laborer Sancho Panza as his squire. The book is considered a founding work of Western literature and the first modern novel, and it is one of the most-translated books in the world. Its influence reached 19th-century French literature, including *[[The Three Musketeers]]* (1844) by [[Alexandre Dumas]], and the word quixotic, meaning "impractically idealistic," entered the language. [[Mark Twain]] said the novel had "swept the world's admiration for the medieval chivalry-silliness out of existence."

American comedian and actor known for insult comedy. A longtime headline performer in [[Las Vegas]] hotel-casinos, he was a frequent guest on *The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson* and *Late Show with David Letterman*. He voiced Mr. Potato Head in the first three films of *[[Toy Story]]*. His film roles include *Run Silent, Run Deep* (1958), *Kelly's Heroes* (1970) and *Casino* (1995). He won a Primetime Emmy Award for the documentary *Mr. Warmth: The Don Rickles Project*.

Fifth-longest river in Europe, flowing about 1,870 km from central Russia to the [[Sea of Azov]]. It rises near Novomoskovsk, and its final stretch, an [[Estuary|estuary]], runs west-southwest. The main city on the river is [[Rostov-on-Don]]. Its basin covers about 425,600 sq km, 87 percent of it in Russia. The river has been a commercial and strategic artery since at least the 9th century, and traders from the [[Byzantine Empire]] used it. The 101 km Volga–Don Canal, completed in 1952, connects the river with the [[Volga]]. The lower Don is associated with the Don Cossacks, a semi-autonomous community of warriors and settlers that emerged in the 16th century.

Disney cartoon character, an anthropomorphic white duck created by [[Walt Disney]] and Dick Lundy. He first appeared in the *Silly Symphony* short *The Wise Little Hen* (1934), and in the 1930s he was a temperamental foil to [[Mickey Mouse]]. His own film series, which introduced Daisy Duck and often featured his nephews Huey, Dewey and Louie, ran until 1961. He appeared in more than 150 animated shorts. *Der Fuehrer's Face* (1943), a satirical [[Propaganda|propaganda]] film set in [[Nazi Germany]], won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Animated Short Film. In comics, Carl Barks expanded Donald's world, creating his rich uncle Scrooge McDuck.

American actor and musician who records as Childish Gambino. He played Troy Barnes on the [[NBC]] sitcom *Community* and created, starred in and directed the FX series *Atlanta*, which won him two Primetime Emmy Awards and two Golden Globe Awards. His films include *Solo: A Star Wars Story* (2018) and *The Lion King* (2019), in which he voiced adult Simba. His single "This Is America" (2018) won four [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]], including Record of the Year and Song of the Year.

American computer scientist and mathematician, professor emeritus at [[Stanford University]]. Knuth has been called the "father of the analysis of [[Algorithm|algorithms]]." He developed rigorous techniques for analyzing computational complexity and popularized asymptotic notation. He received the 1974 ACM Turing Award, informally considered the [[Nobel Prize]] of [[Computer science|computer science]]. His multivolume *The Art of Computer Programming*, begun in 1962, is a comprehensive treatment of fundamental algorithms. He created the TeX typesetting system, the METAFONT font language and the Computer Modern typefaces, as well as the WEB and CWEB systems for literate programming. He has publicly opposed software patents.
